national.title: Anthropic previews Claude Duet personal AI agent for subscribers
national.summary: Anthropic said Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for paying subscribers. Here's what it can do.
national.body: Anthropic has joined the race to develop AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of humans with Claude Duet, a new app it previewed this week.The agent competes with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, rival developers' agents that are already popular with consumers. Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for Claude U.S. Pro and Max subscribers, according to Anthropic.What can Claude Duet do? Claude Duet works as a "proactive agent" for human customers, taking autonomous actions to complete tasks assigned to it."It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said, noting that it was designed for professionals and small business owners "with more on their plates than they can track."Anthropic said Claude Duet's utility lies in its superior judgment, describing it as smart enough to know what to prioritize and which tasks require a user's attention. Each morning, Claude Duet sends its user a daily brief outlining the day's most important items. For the agent to have context, it must be connected to a person's apps, like their email accounts and calendars. Some security professionals have raised concerns about new AI agents' access to such information, warning users to limit how much they share."Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work," Anthropic said.What about security issues?Anthropic highlighted built-in security measures that it says make the app safe to use, noting that the agent never directly sees a person's passwords or sign-in tokens.Claude Duet can also handle administrative tasks like scheduling meetings and creating financial or sales forecasts. It can build web apps, too, Anthropic said. It can draft job postings or make purchases on a business owner's behalf. Anthropic researchers who have tested the app have used it to manage their to-do lists, build apps, schedule interviews and more. How do you sign up?Anthropic said people can sign up on the waitlist at its Claude Duet product page.Invitations are issued in waves, and the product is only available in the U.S. during its research preview, the company said."We're adding people gradually, and you'll get an email when it's your turn," the company said.

national.title: Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster', White House says
national.summary: Ukraine and Russia have not confirmed the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.
national.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.

The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October, though Ukraine and Russia have so far not commented.

"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added.

Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.

The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".

national.body: The tanker involved in an oil spill off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has been identified, according to analysts who spoke to the Reuters new agency. Emirati authorities have not named the vessel, but Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, told Reuters the oil slick was coming from a vessel called the Gem No. 2. Another analyst told the news agency that satellite imagery appears to show a large spill coming from the tanker. "The slick is considerably larger, covering approximately 160 square km (60 square miles), and looks to be coming from the ship," Leon Moreland, a researcher at ⁠the Conflict and Environment Observatory, said. "Furthermore, a slick this close to shore increases the chance it could impact nearby beaches and ecologically sensitive habitats," he said. The Gem No. 2 was hit by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE on Oct. 9, shipping sources told Reuters. No group claimed responsibility for the incident at the time, but maritime security sources told the news agency that it took place outside of the Strait of Hormuz.

national.title: Two Israeli soldiers killed in attack by suspected Palestinian gunmen in West Bank
national.summary: The two attackers were shot dead after a gun battle outside Hebron, four days before Israel's general election.
national.body:
Two Israeli soldiers have been killed in a shooting by two suspected Palestinian attackers in the occupied West Bank, the Israeli military says.

Three other Israelis were wounded in the attack before the gunmen were shot dead at a checkpoint at the entrance of the city of Hebron, officials say.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would "destroy" the Hebron neighbourhood that the two attackers originated from, and that Israel was ready for "extensive action" in the West Bank.

The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.

Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen. Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.

The attack has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning.

Speaking from the scene of the attack, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it".

It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as "collective punishment".

national.summary: First lady Melania Trump's office says she secured a localized ceasefire for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
national.body: First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons. In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29. Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine. The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.""The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary.""Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said. national.title: Six shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
national.summary: Another 28 people are injured in the southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.
national.body:
Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.

Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.

The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car and began shooting inside the church before fleeing the scene.

Security forces have been deployed to the area after the "heinous" attack, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said.

Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.

He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.

CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.

Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.

national.title: Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China's Tibet region
national.summary: Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media.
national.body:
BEIJING (AP) — Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media.

The disaster struck Nagqu, a city north of Tibet's capital Lhasa that's some 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level, on Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, and officials told journalists they were concerned about further building collapses from aftershocks, as well as casualties from rockslides.

WATCH: Wall of mud and debris floods communities in Nepal and Tibet

Search and rescue efforts are complicated by the geography and low temperatures, officials said. As of Friday afternoon, rescuers had done three rounds of searches, going through each household, and each village, said Dunzhu, the acting mayor of Nagqu city, said in a press conference.

More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 2,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,400 tents and 2,000 folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu. It put the earthquake's depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles).

The U.S. agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to its website.

China's official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.

national.title: PSG v Lyon moved as Paris prepares for more protests
national.summary: Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon at the Parc des Princes is pushed back 24 hours as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.
national.body:
Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon has been pushed back 24 hours to Monday as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.

The fixture at the Parc des Princes in Paris had been scheduled to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Sunday but will instead take place at 20:30 on Monday.

The Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) announced the postponement in a statement , external on Friday after French police prohibited the fixture from taking place on its original date.

French authorities are preparing a major security operation for demonstrations planned for Saturday.

Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday to protest rising fuel prices, education standards and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.

Marches took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions and student groups, and were marred by some incidents of violence, looting and destruction.

The security challenge is further complicated by Sunday's NFL match between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France, an event expected to require a significant police deployment.

The game will be played in Saint-Denis, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where the protests are expected to begin.

national.title: Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia
national.summary: When an outbreak strikes, humans try to avoid germs. (Remember wiping off groceries at the start of the pandemic?) What about ... monkeys?
national.body:
One of the macaques at a Texas sanctuary, where researchers ran tests to see if the monkeys became germaphobes after experiencing a viral outbreak. Stephan Kaufhold hide caption

In the very early days of COVID-19, millions who'd rarely thought twice about germ avoidance became germophobes.

Some folks wiped down groceries before stuffing them into the refrigerator. Others let mail quarantine outside for days lest it harbor stray viruses. With the hindsight that SARS-CoV-2 spread primarily through the air, these sorts of precautions seem extreme. But in the moment, they were perhaps reasonable ways of avoiding an unknown pathogen.

Around this same time, a different virus hit a macaque sanctuary in Texas. New research suggests the monkeys responded in similar ways as humans did to COVID-19 — by being extra germophobic.

Humans are far from the only animals to avoid possible sources of disease. Scientists have found that critters as diverse as monkeys and nematodes (aka roundworms) can sense and steer clear of feces, for instance, which can harbor harmful bacteria.

"Something that has been less studied is the question of how flexible this avoidance is," says Stephan Kaufhold , a cognitive scientist at UC San Diego. He wanted to see if experiencing an outbreak could make individual monkeys even more wary of picking up pathogens.

The outbreak in the Texas sanctuary, home to over 100 macaques, offered Kaufhold and his colleagues an opportunity to put that question to the test.

In 2020, macaques in an enclosure at the sanctuary started getting sick with an HIV-like virus called SRV.

national.title: Deadly shooting near Paris investigated as 'crime of terrorism', minister says
national.summary: One person is killed and five wounded in a series of attacks and the suspected gunman has been apprehended.
national.body:
One person has been killed and five others wounded - three seriously - in a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which authorities are investigating as "terrorism".

Several drive-by shootings took place on Friday - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière. The rampage lasted almost 15 minutes, said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. A12-year-old girl is among the wounded.

The suspected attacker has been arrested. The motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".

Nuñez told reporters in Trappes: "It's clearly a terrorist crime, that's what [the prosecutor] has said."

The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.

The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.

The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière.

A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.

national.title: Delicate operation carried out on explosives-packed WWII shipwreck
national.summary: Engineers sprang into action amid concern that an 82-year-old WWII shipwreck's crumbling masts could topple and set off its 1,500-ton sunken explosives payload.
national.body: Sheerness, England — A delicate operation aimed at preventing an 82-year-old U.S. shipwreck packed with tons of World War II explosives from unleashing a potentially catastrophic tidal wave on London has been completed. But while the most imminent danger has been addressed, the explosives remain inside the rusting wreck of the SS Richard Montgomery on the riverbed, and experts aren't taking their eyes off it.The Montgomery, one of about 2,700 Liberty ships built in the U.S. to support the Allied war effort, was grounded on a sandbar off the town of Sheerness in the Thames Estuary, just 40 miles from the British capital, in August 1944. It was carrying munitions intended to support the Allies following the D-Day landings.The vessel broke apart during salvage efforts and sank, with an estimated 1,500 tons of explosives in its cargo holds.The ship's three rusting masts protruding from the water had been a familiar sight to residents and passing vessels for decades. But recent surveys revealed increasing deterioration in the structure, raising fears the masts could collapse and trigger an explosion."The vessel was starting to lean and deteriorate, so they could see some of the structures around the mast starting to collapse," Nolan Conway, a naval architect with Florida-based marine salvage firm Resolve Marine Group, which was contracted to remove the masts, told CBS News."The fear is the masts could have fallen onto the cargo itself, causing it to detonate," he said. "Some of the munitions are believed to be fused munitions with pressure fuses, so something like an impact could potentially set them off."U.K. maritime minister Keir Mather told lawmakers in the House of Commons this week that the "complex project requiring specialist program, engineering and risk management expertise" had been completed ahead of schedule and on budget, with all three of the masts removed at a cost of just under $13 million, according to The Guardian.Mather said in the U.K. Parliament that the masts had put "significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site."The government has long maintained an exclusion zone around the wreck, which is about 1.5 miles off the Sheerness coast. national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — First lady Melania Trump has brokered an upcoming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the war-ravaged city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, the White House announced on Friday.

The White House said that the first lady had initiated the discussions and that she and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire. There has been no immediate comment from the Ukrainian or Russian governments.

Trump has made children in conflict one of her signature issues as first lady, hosting a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. She also has personally written to Russian President Vladimir Putin to work to reunite children displaced by the war with their families.

WATCH: U.S. must put pressure on Russia so Putin ends the war, Ukrainian official says

Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. There's no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Menacing drones buzz overhead. Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. Further calamity struck in June 2023, when floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military, killing hundreds of residents. Those left in the battered city along Ukraine's southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, which as the occupying power is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive, had made no commitment.

national.body:
A first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States under a new import agreement has set sail, the Kremlin said Friday, two weeks after President Donald Trump said he struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin despite Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.

"The first oil tanker has sailed off to customers, and regular supplies will continue," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said without elaborating.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said earlier this week that the first shipment would amount to 40,000 tons of diesel, according to Russia's Interfax news agency.

Marine intelligence firm Kpler said the vessel was signaling it was headed to New York to arrive Nov. 7 and would be the first Russian diesel delivery to the United States since July 2023.

The abrupt reversal of U.S. sanctions policy on Russia over its invasion of its neighbor was seen as an attempt by Trump to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

WATCH: Tightening sanctions on Russia is 'the way to end this war,' says David Kramer

The diesel shipment of 40,000 tons amounts to around 300,000 barrels, or about 7% of the roughly 4 million barrels of diesel the U.S. economy consumes in a single day.

The import agreement, which Trump says foresees millions more tons of Russian diesel reaching the U.S. in coming months, is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing.

The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes.

With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".

Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.

Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well – relying on medication to get rest.

national.summary: Nigeria this week recorded its first case of Ebola in the current outbreak, which has spread from the epicenter in Congo to several other African countries.
national.body:
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.

Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.

She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.

Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Global Health 'I've never seen anything like this' — A U.S. doctor treats Ebola's youngest victims Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.

Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.

The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.

national.title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
national.summary: Once the world's largest producer of mink pelts, the nation's industry has declined in recent years.
national.body:
Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.

Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.

The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.

Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.

"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.

The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.

However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.

Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".

national.title: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted
national.summary: Issues remain with the network used by the Ukrainian military, sources say, after repeated denials of a deliberate slowdown.
national.body:
Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits on the satellite uplink had been reversed by Elon Musk.

The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations.

The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back".

Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.

The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks.

They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted".

Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said.

Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues.

national.title: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
national.summary: Social media sites aren't the biggest fans of people leaving via hyperlinks. In fact, Meta has made it subscription-worthy for a Facebook Page to post more than two hyperlinks per month. What's the rationale for companies want to keep you on their site?
national.body:
Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.

In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?

What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.

Meta has limited how many hyperlinks Facebook Pages can post through a subscription Tony Avelar/AP Photo hide caption

Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."

What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!

local.title: Collection that showcases Rochester's Puerto Rican history is being preserved
local.summary: The University of Rochester's Department of Rare Books, Special Collection and Preservation acquired a collection from Henry Ignacio Padrón-Morales, a longtime activist, educator, musician and poet.
local.body:
Decades of work documenting Rochester's Puerto Rican community, arts collaborations and bilingual education are now preserved in a University of Rochester archive.

The collection belongs to Henry Ignacio Padrón-Morales , a longtime activist, educator, musician and poet who moved to Rochester as a teenager in the late 1960s and became a leader in Rochester's Latino community.

"I have grown more accepting of the fact that Rochester is my home," Padrón-Morales said. "I'm from here. I am from here. I've given this place a chunk of my life, and that is important in and of itself to have had that growth because I'll talk to people and you know they're from here, they're everywhere, but after being here this long, I consider Rochester as my home."

Over the years, Padrón-Morales has worn many different hats in Rochester, working as an educator in the Rochester City School District, a community advocate, and most recently co-owner of Hipocampo Children's Bookstore .

His work documenting the city's Puerto Rican community and its cultural and educational history is now in the care of the University of Rochester's Department of Rare Books, Special Collections and Preservation. The university acquired his documents for its archives, cataloging them as the "Henry I. Padrón-Morales papers."

The collection documents Padrón-Morales' work as an activist, organizer, artist, collaborator, volunteer and advocate for Puerto Rico and Rochester's Latino community.

"I was like gripping it, like you know, not out of total distrust, but out of some distrust in what would happen with it. How would it be treated? And not today, as I've seen, it's in a good beginning stage, and in good hands," Padrón-Morales told WXXI News.

Conversations about archiving his work began in 2025 when Molly Ball, associate professor of history at the University of Rochester, applied for a historic preservation grant through the Rochester Area Community Foundation.

local.title: Greece schools seek sustainable solutions to meet vulnerable students' needs
local.summary: The Greece Central School District is looking for long term solutions to meet a growing need for specialized instruction for students.
local.body:
Listen • 1:08 The Greece Central School District is looking for long term solutions to meet a growing need for specialized instruction for students.

Assistant Superintendent Michael Zaffuts outlined three key areas of need — space for special education instruction, funding for a program designed for vulnerable students — for instance who have mental illness diagnoses, low grades, or are chronically absent — and adjustments to account for shifting enrollment at schools.

"These long-standing challenges led us to a place where we felt like we needed a long-term systemic effort to try to tackle them to represent not only solutions to those problems but also what our community values and matching a solution to those and a path forward with what our community values," Zaffuts said at a school board meeting Tuesday.

Special education enrollment at Greece schools is up by about 150 students compared with five years ago.

"We currently have services being delivered in hallways and cafeterias on a regular basis, and we need to figure out what is a long-term and viable solution to support those students and staff members," Zaffuts said, referring to the increased enrollment of students who need specialized instruction.

The district's Alcott Road campus is also in need of long-term financial support he said. The campus houses programs like Phoenix Academy which provides trauma-sensitive support for high schoolers, GED classes, and tutoring.

The district is working with consultants at Leadership Solutions Advisors to find potential solutions. The school board expects to hear about next steps on Dec. 1, followed by a presentation of three possible pathways by June.

"It's a huge undertaking, and it's something that everyone will have to kind of adjust in certain ways," School board member Mary Lyke said. "But I think for the district in the long run, it's just such a healthy thing to do."

local.title: With lockout looming, World Series could be last games for a while
local.summary: MILWAUKEE — On the eve of the World Series, there is a realization these may be Major League Baseball’s last games for a while. Owners are pushing for a salary cap, and that could prompt a lockout starting Dec. 2 and result in canceled games in 2027. “It would be a real bummer to lose […]
local.body:
MILWAUKEE -- On the eve of the World Series, there is a realization these may be Major League Baseball’s last games for a while.

Owners are pushing for a salary cap, and that could prompt a lockout starting Dec. 2 and result in canceled games in 2027.

“It would be a real bummer to lose a season, that’s for sure,” Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen said Thursday ahead of the World Series opener against Milwaukee. “I think the industry as a whole is in way too good of a place.”

This year’s World Series is the first since 1991 between teams both in the bottom half of payrolls: Milwaukee ranked 19th as of Aug. 31 and Tampa Bay 25th. MLB says a cap is needed to help all teams compete more consistently, but players contend because of the method owners use to define expenses, a cap would lead to management taking a greater share of the sport’s revenue.

“The system that’s being proposed, which is similar to other leagues in terms of revenue-sharing system, not only will help us compete, but more importantly all of the teams with lower payrolls, too, which is something also I think the fans want,” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said.

MLB’s proposal would cap spending in 2027 at $245.3 million using figures for luxury tax payrolls, and limit a player to 15% of a team’s payroll. Free agents would be capped at $265 million over six seasons -- far under Juan Soto’s record $765 million, 15-year deal with the New York Mets.

“If they’re going to sit there and wave their little magic wand at us saying they’re going to get a salary cap, it’s not going to happen,” Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill said.

Negotiations for a collective bargaining agreement to replace the five-year deal expiring Dec. 1 could turn into each side trying to outlast the other.

local.title: Silver Creek receives clean audit report
local.summary: SILVER CREEK — The Silver Creek Central School District received a clean, unmodified opinion of its finances in an Independent Audit Report through the end of last school year. The district discussed the results of the report at a recent Board of Education meeting. The report was conducted by certif
local.body:
SILVER CREEK -- The Silver Creek Central School District received a clean, unmodified opinion of its finances in an Independent Audit Report through the end of last school year. The district discussed the results of the report at a recent Board of Education meeting.

The report was conducted by certified public accountants Buffamante, Whipple, Buttafaro, for the period ending June 30. Matt Miller, Business Office Manager, was commended for his work by the Board and Superintendent Dr. Katie Ralston, who said the positive report is "truly an accomplishment".

The district was, however, cited for having far too much money deemed as unassigned fund balance. As a result, a corrective action plan was required to address the district's unassigned funds of $6,537,152, which equates to approximately 19.6% of the 2026-27 school budget. The state legal limit is 4%, but districts across the state often exceed that figure. Silver Creek's unassigned fund balance in the previous year's report was roughly 15%.

Ralston clarified the excess fund balance is not unused tax revenue or "extra money" the district has at its disposal. Rather, it is what she called a "complicated calculation" of budget transfers regarding money allocated to the district's 2024 Capital Project. While the project was approved in 2024, the invoices for the work come in as the work is done, meaning the funds must be available to pay the bills throughout the project.

Ralston said the amount of unassigned fund balance "is not because it can be used for anything that we want it to be. It is not because we are squirreling away money. It is because it's a very designated and intentional use for our Capital Improvement Project and our vehicle purchases."

The $36.1 million Capital Project is the largest Capital Project in the school's history. The project was fully funded through capital reserves and state aid reimbursement, resulting in no tax increase to residents. Approximately $5.8 million of reserve funds were moved between accounts to cover Capital Project costs. A capital reserve fund was dissolved, resulting in additional revenue to the district.

The report also found no compliance issues or any general control issues in its single audit of the district's Impact Aid funds. A single audit was required due to the amount of federal funds received by the district this past year.

Also at the recent meeting, Desiree Clarke was appointed as Internal Claims Auditor for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Kelly Imhoff was provisionally appointed as a 12-month Clerk II at a rate of $16.25 per hour. Brookelynn Wood resigned as a 10-Month Cleaner.

OBSERVER Photo by Christian Storms Randolph captain Gavin Senn, center, is congratulated by teammates Grady Steward, left, and Chris Reynolds after scoring the game-winning goal against Portville in the Section VI Class C quarterfinals at Allegany-Limestone High School on Thursday.

ALLEGANY -- After leveling the score in the 64th minute, Portville continued its relentless attack toward the Randolph goal seeking the winner in the Section VI Class C boys soccer quarterfinals.

Watching Tanner Patterson's free kick sail into the Portville box during the 71st minute, Randolph senior Gavin Senn patiently waited for his moment and, after Grady Steward knocked the ball out of the scrum, Senn made his move with a quick strike that put the Cardinals ahead for good, 2-1 on Thursday night at Allegany-Limestone High School.

"The wind was definitely a factor," Randolph head coach Dave Pihlblad stated. "We had to go into it in the second half with a 1-0 lead and Portville was all over us for the first 15-20 minutes of the half. They got that goal and deep down inside I didn't have a good feeling because we weren't creating and they were all over us. Then just one moment, it's in the back of the net and we held on for dear life the last 10 minutes there."

The Cardinals regained the lead less than 10 minutes after Portville's Colin German leveled the score at 1-1, finishing a great run shooting back to the left while dribbling past the Randolph defense. With Portville already in control of the momentum much of the second half, German's goal tipped the scales even further and the Cardinals looked to be hanging on for overtime.

Instead, it was Randolph getting that next goal and the Cardinals really put the pressure on their Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Athletic Association Division II rival to score again in the final nine minutes.

local.title: Other views: AI will demand a return sooner or later
local.summary: It’s too soon to call what happened this week to artificial intelligence stocks a correction. Call it instead a reminder: Hype about new technologies is an inevitable human temptation, and sometimes it pays off, but eventually investors demand returns on capital. That’s the way to think about the di
local.body:
It's too soon to call what happened this week to artificial intelligence stocks a correction. Call it instead a reminder: Hype about new technologies is an inevitable human temptation, and sometimes it pays off, but eventually investors demand returns on capital.

That's the way to think about the disconcerting market swings of recent days. Many tech shares have taken a dive, sometimes by large percentages. That has dragged down the NASDAQ and the S&P 500 index, which has come to be dominated by those companies. Our advice is to go for a relaxing walk this weekend instead of checking your 401(k) balance.

This seems counterintuitive in the face of encouraging earnings reports from some big AI-related companies, and in some cases the good earnings news arrested the decline in the company's stock price. But stock prices are forward rather than backward looking, and investors still are grappling with big questions about the AI future.

AI will have a profound effect on the global economy. It remains impossible to say what those effects might be or who will profit from them, and how. Estimates of global AI-related investments regularly top $1 trillion per year and probably are undercounts after including other forms of investment such as the companies that adopt AI in their own businesses.

This implies that AI would need to substantially boost business productivity and generate unprecedented returns eventually. One recent academic study calculated that American data-center hyperscalers alone would need to earn revenue equal to roughly 9% of gross domestic product per year by 2032 to break even on their investments.

America's ability to raise and allocate this private capital--the institutional investors and entrepreneurs, the legal system and market structure--is the envy of the world. But unforgiving market discipline on the way down is a not-so-secret ingredient in the special sauce.

As AI continues to evolve, the challenge will be to reevaluate the risks and do so relative to other bets. It's a continuous process that plays out every second markets are open.

Investors this week didn't abandon equities entirely, even if they did pour some capital back into the bond market. Instead, they pivoted into recently overlooked industries such as consumer goods. The Dow Jones Industrial Average had a decent week.

The outcome could have implications for religious freedom, parental rights and public health nationwide.The legal fight comes as the country faces its largest measles outbreak in a generation, with cases spreading in Amish communities and other parts of the United States.The town of Clymer, in Chautauqua County, is home to one of New York's largest Amish populations.It's where Joseph Miller's children attended Shady Lane School, an Amish-run school that was fined $20,000 by the state Health Department in 2022 for failing to comply with New York's school vaccination requirements.Miller and other plaintiffs challenged the state's policy, saying they "possess fervent religious objections to injecting their children with vaccines."Their argument centers in part on the state's allowance for medical exemptions while prohibiting religious exemptions."There is a medical exemption, right, that students, parents can opt out based on medical reasons and therefore, if you can opt out for medical reasons, you should be allowed to opt out for religious reasons," said legal analyst Michael Macomber, who is a partner and CEO at Tully Rinckey PLLC.Macomber said the plaintiffs' argument is that the state's vaccination requirements are not sufficiently neutral under the Constitution.New York, meanwhile, has argued that the requirements are public health measures that apply to students regardless of their religious beliefs."New York's taking the position, this is a health requirement. It has to do with physical health and safety. It's neutral on its face. It applies to everyone. It has nothing to do with the free exercise of religion," Macomber said.The lawsuit first went before a federal judge in the Western District of New York. She ruled against the Amish plaintiffs, citing legal precedent upholding a similar vaccine requirement in Connecticut.The plaintiffs appealed to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, which also ruled against them.They then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the case. local.title: Niagara Falls continues Main Street revitalization; unveils Niagara University housing plan
local.summary: Niagara Falls unveiled plans to turn a Main Street building that has been vacant for decades into Niagara University student housing, as plans to revitalize dozens of properties in the corridor continue.
local.body: Niagara Falls unveiled plans to turn a Main Street building that has been vacant for decades into Niagara University student housing, as plans to revitalize dozens of properties in the corridor continue.For decades, several blocks of Main Street in Niagara Falls have been left to rot, but in 2024, plans were announced to redevelop several long-forgotten buildings.WATCH: Niagara Falls continues Main Street revitalization; unveils Niagara University housing plan“It’s not going to be the Main Street of our childhood. It’s going to be better,” Mayor Robert Restaino said in 2024.He and the City of Niagara Falls acquired 38 Main Street properties, between Ontario Avenue and Michigan Avenue, from absentee landlords to resell them to new developers through incentivized deals. Restaino said the city has made deals for a little less than half of the 38 total properties. These properties carry so many memories for residents, like Jenss Department Store or The Rapids Theater.“I would say we are at least in the 20s of properties we still have that we’re looking to develop,” Restaino said. “And now, what was the initial, I would say, linchpin or centerpiece of what we hope to do on Main Street is happening.”The centerpiece that he referred to is 2018 and 2010 Main Street, a building that has been boarded up since, at the very least, 2007.Developer Abe Bose announced plans to invest $25 million into the building to transform it into Niagara University student housing. He said that it would host 100 units of student housing and commercial space.“It’s not just about replacing blighted structures with modern, premium student housing and ground-floor retail. It’s about creating an economic engine that brings foot traffic and daily activity back to this block,” Bose said.While that is a nice addition, Restaino hopes it will be a catalyst to find even more developers.“Collectively, there’s in excess of $50 million of private investment here,” Restaino said.Projects underway include both market rate apartments and commercial buildings. They have various completion dates, but Restaino hopes to see the Niagara University housing open late 2028.Join the Niagara County Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.

local.title: Buffalo voters to decide 11 proposed city charter changes
local.summary: Beyond the candidates on the ballot, Buffalo voters will also decide on 11 proposed changes to the City of Buffalo Charter.
local.body: Beyond the candidates on the ballot, Buffalo voters will also decide on 11 proposed changes to the City of Buffalo Charter.A sample ballot shows the 11 charter questions take up about a third of the front of the ballot and the entire back.The City Charter essentially serves as the rulebook for Buffalo city government, outlining how it operates and what it can and cannot do.Laurence Rubin, chairman of the City of Buffalo Charter Revision Commission, said the proposals allow residents to have a say in how their local government operates.“It's important because it's giving the citizens of Buffalo an opportunity to speak about their constitution, their local constitution,” Rubin said. WATCH: Buffalo voters to decide 11 proposed city charter changesThe Buffalo Common Council created the Charter Revision Commission and held public hearings to discuss and fine-tune the proposed changes.Rubin said many of the questions examined by the commission were prompted by issues that surfaced when Chris Scanlon took over as acting mayor following Byron Brown's departure.“There were issues like, is he really the acting mayor or just has the powers of a mayor, and what happened to his council seat,” Rubin said. But the proposed changes go well beyond questions surrounding mayoral succession and cover a wide range of issues involving city government.“It affects everything from how they participate in voting, to how the budget is made, to how citizens participate in advisory boards, to issues like how the police are serving the community, to dealing with issues about whether or not human rights are being affected in the City of Buffalo,” Rubin said.Early voting starts Saturday. Voters interested in learning more about each of the 11 proposed charter changes can review more information from the City of Buffalo Charter Revision Commission. The city's commission page includes information designed to help understand the proposals.Rubin said he hopes voters turn out and make their voices heard on the questions found on the back of the ballot.“I would hope that people will vote. I hope people come out and vote in general, right? That's our civic duty, and I hope they flip the page and vote for everything,” Rubin said.

entertainment.summary: The tech giant does not have an ad tier on its Apple TV streaming service, but one of the company's top ad execs tells THR that F1 is growing its share of the pie.
entertainment.body:
F1, Teresi notes, attracts an upscale audience, which Teresi notes that studies show has a higher median income than other major sports like the NFL or NBA, which in turn is bringing in premium brands.

Indeed, for its first season with F1, Apple secured significant deals with American Express and Ford, with both brands expressing enthusiasm as the tech company begins to think about selling its second season with the sport.

“With Ford’s return to F1, we’re meeting fans where they are and telling our story in a bigger way than ever,” said Will Ford, GM of Ford Racing. “ Apple TV is a tremendous partner in helping us reach new audiences, and we’re already seeing stronger awareness of Ford Racing and Ford’s leadership in innovation. As we celebrate 125 years of racing at Ford, we’re focused on leading the next generation of motorsport fandom and culture, and Apple TV is a key partner for us in doing this.”

The ads, Teresi notes, are thoughtfully integrated so as not to distract from the racing, and the company worked with existing F1 sponsors (who are already featured on cars and uniforms) as it pursued deals.

Eddy Cue, the Apple executive who oversees its entire services business, said that viewership of F1 on Apple TV is up double digits compared to ESPN last season. Those numbers are still modest compared to, say, the NFL (ESPN averaged 1.3 million viewers in its final season with F1), but with a younger, wealthier and more engaged audience, Teresi nonetheless says that it is having a meaningful impact on Apple’s ad ambitions.

But that doesn’t mean it isn’t working towards Apple’s goal of creating a meaningful ad business that still works within its ethos of creating great experiences, something that other ad-supported product are not always the best at.

entertainment.title: Fashion Is the Future of Technology: How V of BTS, Navy Blue, Kelela and Nothing Are Bridging Tech and Culture — ‘Find Joy in the Little Things’
entertainment.summary: As technology becomes an extension of personal style, Nothing, Navy Blue and Kelela explore the intersection of design, self-expression and the future of music.
entertainment.body:
Technology and fashion have always been intertwined, but as more of the devices we use become things we wear, the line between the two is getting harder to distinguish. Explore BTS V Kelela See latest videos, charts and news

Headphones are an obvious example. Once primarily functional accessories, they’ve become part of how people present themselves in public. Whether worn over the ears, resting around the neck, or sitting on a purse or a hat, they can complement an outfit, communicate personal taste and signal an affinity for a particular brand or community. Like sneakers, jewelry, socks or a favorite bag, they’re increasingly part of the visual language through which people express themselves and story tell. Related 'Thursday Night Football' 2026: Where to Livestream New England Patriots vs. Chicago Bears Game Online 'ACOTAR' Book 6 Is Almost Here: Everything to Know About Sarah J. Maas' Next Two Books From Adorable to Absurd, Shop Last-Minute 'KPop Demon Hunters' Halloween Costumes Online

And it makes sense. When technology becomes something you physically wear, its design becomes part of your appearance. You’re not just choosing a device for what it can do. You’re choosing something that will exist on your body, in public, alongside everything else you use to communicate who you are and what you’re about. And now you’re thinking, “Will these headphones match most of my looks? Will these headphones bring my fits together or take away from them?”

We’re at a point where so many headphones have amazing noise-canceling, transparency mode, great audio quality and mics. Some may be better than others in some categories but the differences — no matter if the brands like it or not — are becoming few and far between.

That raises a bigger question about the future of technology: As products become increasingly capable, will their cultural significance matter as much as their technical capabilities?

At Nothing’s New Noise event in New York, that question extended beyond the products on display. The event brought together technology, fashion and music, with conversations featuring Kelela and Navy Blue — two artists whose approaches to music and fashion offer different perspectives on where culture is heading.

The connection isn’t simply that musicians are wearing headphones or that technology companies are borrowing from fashion. It’s that technology, fashion and music are increasingly intertwined forms of self-expression. The products we carry, the clothes we wear and the music we listen to all contribute to how we construct our identities and how people construct identities for us. And as technology becomes more visible in our everyday lives, the way it looks, feels and fits into our personal worlds becomes harder to separate from its function.

entertainment.title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Nicholas Galitzine and Bill Skarsgard in Peter Berg’s Technically Impressive, Emotionally Hollow Netflix War Drama
entertainment.summary: Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis also star in the AFI Fest-premiering film, inspired by the true story of a football game played between Marines stationed in the Pacific theater of WWII.
entertainment.body:
The Mosquito Bowl , Peter Berg ’s new World War II drama for Netflix, sets the tone right away with a famous Herbert Hoover quote. “Older men declare war,” it goes. “But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war.”

It is a statement eternal in its truth and devastating in its poignancy, one well worth keeping in mind any time the specter of battle is raised. It is also, you may have noticed, the theme of more or less every single war movie ever made. It would take some really sharp and distinctive execution to make it feel fresh again — and as admirable as The Mosquito Bowl often is in its craft, its storytelling falls well short of that bar. Related Stories Movies Friday Night Fights: Peter Berg Returns to Football ... and War Movies Peter Berg's Netflix War Movie 'The Mosquito Bowl' to Premiere at AFI Fest (Exclusive) The Mosquito Bowl The Bottom Line Looks good but says little. Venue: AFI Fest Release date: Friday, Oct. 30 Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgard, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg, Mark L. Smith Rated R, 2 hours 6 minutes

The premise, at least, had potential. Adapted from the book of the same title by Buzz Bissinger (whose Friday Night Lights also spawned a Berg film), The Mosquito Bowl leads up to a legendary football game played between two Marine divisions while stationed at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve in 1944. One would expect the sports angle to add a welcome new spin on the usual war-drama storylines — and it does, though not nearly as much as you’re probably guessing, given how little of the 126-minute run time the match actually takes up.

Its leads are a quartet of elite college football players who’ve joined the Marines after the 1941 bombing of Pearl Harbor, and all are played by hot rising stars du jour: the ubiquitous but apparently un – typecast – able Nicholas Galitzine as thoughtful Brown alum John McLaughry; Ray Nicholson as charming Purdue alum turned promising NFL draftee Tony Butkovich; Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgard as anxious David Schreiner and wild Bob Bauman, both graduates of University of Wisconsin (though only David maintains a grudge against Tony for beating them in a pivotal game).

But if that Hoover epigraph suggests a well-trod path, the rest of the film confirms it has no intention of straying from it. entertainment.title: Tony Dokoupil Has a Question: Will You Watch His New Podcast? (Exclusive)
entertainment.summary: The 'CBS Evening News' anchor is nearly a year into his tenure, and launching the show's first big digital expansion, 'Great Question with Tony Dokoupil.'
entertainment.body:
Tony Dokoupil is launching a podcast, and if you happen to watch the video version and look very, very closely, there’s a chance you could spot Salvador Dali’s phone number.

Dokoupil, the anchor of the CBS Evening News , is now almost 11 months into the job, and to hear him explain it, he is just beginning to find his rhythm and footing in the high-profile role. So that makes for an opportune moment to expand the Evening News to digital platforms with a wholly original podcast extension: Great Question with Tony Dokoupil .

It will be available in video form (on YouTube and all the other podcast platforms), shot in his office, alongside audio versions.

“You’re going to get to see my dad’s mugshot on the shelf behind me [he was arrested for smuggling marijuana in 1992], and my great uncle’s pioneering gay advocacy journal that he came out with called Michael’s Thing on the shelf behind me, and all my old Newsweek covers and a bunch of books I like,” Dokoupil says, noting all the paraphernalia, before landing on his favorite: “I rescued a Rolodex from the dump when Newsweek was on the brink of folding.”

Great Question will be built off of the foundation of the Evening News , but it will also be its own thing. The premise? Twice per week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, Dokoupil will focus on one “great question,” looking to journalists or experts to help answer it.

“When I think of the Evening News , I think of our beat as being the story of America one day at a time, which is why I always have that sign off, ‘that’s another day in America,’ and even though we have this amazing team and these global resources and we put out a jam-packed show, there are still things we couldn’t get to the bottom of, and so every day starts with new questions,” Dokoupil explains. “Over the course of a week, there’ll be things that we didn’t get to or that are lingering, and the hope of the podcast is you’ll be able to distill that into the biggest, most urgent, most pressing, most important, or just most interesting question, and then you try to match that to a guest.”

Among those guests will be author and podcast host Malcolm Gladwell to discuss whether America needs more police and 60 Minutes contributor Gianna Toboni talking about the death penalty. Episodes will focus on why America kids seem so bad at math, if gambling apps are trying to addict us, and other tough or interesting questions.

entertainment.title: Alexander Brothers Case Is a “Microcosm for a Lot of Questions about Sexual Assault,” Says Doc Director
entertainment.summary: 'The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers’ director Emma Schwartz argues the high-profile case would not have come to light without New York’s Adult Survivors Act.
entertainment.body:
Ahead of their sentencing next week in a federal sex-trafficking case, a Peacock documentary is casting a fresh light on the sordid story of the Alexander brothers.

The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers , which premieres on Sunday, arrives just as brothers Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — two of them onetime stars in the flashy world of luxury real estate — face potential life sentences. After being accused of drugging and raping dozens of women in a federal trial earlier this year, they were convicted of sex trafficking, while two of them are still awaiting trial for a state case in Florida.

The three-part documentary follows the brothers’ rise from their privileged youth in Miami to reaching the highest echelons of high-end real estate, first at Douglas Elliman and then at their own brokerage, called Official. And it tracks them through their rapid downfall after news broke that two women had filed civil suits against Oren and Alon alleging rape and assault, after which dozens of women came forward with their own grisly accusations. (The brothers have maintained that they never drugged and raped anyone.)

The Wolves of Real Estate director Emma Schwartz is no newbie to stories of sexual abuse and violence: She executive produced and co-directed The Fall of Diddy for HBO Max, which tracked accusations surrounding Sean “Diddy” Combs. Still, she says, even with her track record in telling tricky pop-culture investigations with the production company Maxine (she also worked on Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV ), “this one was definitely one of the harder ones” in terms of finding subjects willing to go on camera, she told The Hollywood Reporter .

In the interview, Schwartz also discussed a lingering mystery in the brothers’ story, the details of the case that stick with her and the questions that she hopes viewers ask after watching the documentary.

The story has been covered pretty intensely in the press. What more did you feel that a documentary could bring to the story?

I think a lot of the stories that we like to focus on at Maxine are taking a big look at the story. The day-to-day coverage only tells you part of it. And even the articles that went through a dozen accounts in the summer of 2024, they were sort of part of the buildup of a story. And what you can do with a documentary is you can look at the entirety. How did it begin? What happened before? You can look outside of the walls of a criminal case. You’re right, there were reporters at trial writing articles a number of days, but that only told you part of the story. And part of what we can also do is help raise these bigger questions. Why is it that it takes women so long to come forward? What systems do we have in place to enable women to feel safe coming forward? How much does power and wealth play into the way the justice system goes after cases like this? And so I think there’s a lot of bigger questions that you can see in context in a documentary that you might not understand or see [otherwise]. But beyond that, I think there are really unique accounts that we have from individuals that were not necessarily in the public domain that have not been out there that help you understand people’s relationships with the brothers, the kind of power that they wielded and so much more.

entertainment.title: ‘Clueless’ Inspired Kim Kardashian to Buy This Priceless Monet
entertainment.summary: An exclusive excerpt from Jonathan Van Meter’s ‘Citizen Kim’ reveals how a French Impressionist masterpiece ended up on her bathroom wall.
entertainment.body:
One day in early February 2022, I was hanging out at Kim’s office as she tried to cram two cover shoots into one day. Between the shoots, Kim was back in her glam room, getting RE-glammed with different hair and new makeup, this time to shoot the cover of Vogue Hong Kong. Kim was effusive and bossy, running her multibillion-dollar business in a bathrobe, two gay men pulling at her hair and face. At one point, as she was helped into and then out of a complicated, totally sheer Schiaparelli tulle dress — it was pretty much nothing but scaffolding — I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched. Lately, she and I had been playing a little game of “Guess What Happened in 1995?” because we kept being surprised by the astonishing number of cultural and technological shifts — to say nothing of her own complicated personal circumstances — that unfolded in that one year. Once she was dressed and sitting back in her chair, I said to Kim, “You know what else happened in 1995?” She looked at me expectantly. The movie Clueless came out (her favorite film). When it was first released, Kim and her father (and a group of Kim’s friends and their fathers) all went to see it together. “We were dying at every reference,” she told me. “It was so me in high school. … I had pretty much every outfit that the girls wore in Clueless . … I was still into Contempo Casuals and shopping at Judy’s at the Century City Mall. … Like, when I saw that movie, I couldn’t believe it. Clueless is still, to this day, my favorite movie. It really resonated.” Related Stories Lifestyle Kim Kardashian Read Every Page of Her Authorized Biography. Here's What She Pushed Back On. Beyond the Book "Respect Rather Than Reverence": Inside the Making of a Grittier 'Sense and Sensibility'

Clueless , inspired by Jane Austen’s Emma , stars Alicia Silverstone as Cher Horowitz, a ditzy but well-meaning rich girl living in the ultraprivileged bubble of her Beverly Hills high school. “I just wanted this fake world that you would see in a comedy of manners about the turn of the century,” director Amy Heckerling said in an interview, adding, “Positivity fascinates me — I don’t understand it … so I started to think about a character that would be so happy and sure things would work out.”

Clueless was written and directed in 1994, right as Kim was entering her freshman year at Marymount High School, and right as her family was becoming a fixture in the inescapable O.J. Simpson news cycle. Heckerling’s highly tuned antennae capture such a specific moment of Beverly Hills youth culture; it’s hard to believe something of Kim’s life wasn’t absorbed from the ether. Cher goes to the mall and shops at Contempo Casuals and Fred Segal. She is obsessed with her closet, the organization of which puts even Kim to shame. Cher’s iconic yellow plaid outfit evoked Kim’s Catholic school girl uniform as imagined by Donatella Versace. Kim and Kourtney and their friends carpooled to school, blasting hip-hop in a white BMW, while Cher drives her friends in a white Jeep Wrangler. Cher famously volunteers to be “captain of the Pismo Beach disaster relief” effort, while Kim spent Coastal Cleanup Day scouring the Santa Monica beaches for trash. All of the scenes in the ostentatiously enormous house where Cher lives with her strict, attorney father (who happens to look exactly like O.J. lawyer Robert Shapiro) were shot in a 10,000-square-foot house in Encino, just down the road from Robert Kardashian’s 11,000-square-foot former home on Mandalay Drive, which, much like the fictional Horowitz residence, features a grand double staircase. As their homes become the prep site for a big trial, Kim and Cher both take an interest in their father’s legal work. Ripped straight from the headlines, Cher calls her brother-in-law Josh a “Kato” — as in Kato Kaelin, one of the minor witnesses in the O.J. trial — meaning “freeloader.”

entertainment.title: Most Played Track, Biggest Artist & More Key Takeaways From WARM’s 2026 Dance Insights Report
entertainment.summary: WARM ranked the Global Top 100 dance tracks over the first half of 2026 using data from more than 200 dance radio stations in nearly 40 countries.
entertainment.body:
The World Airplay Radio Monitor has released its 2026 H1 Dance Insights report , which compares the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025 across artist performance, label share, collaborations, gender, genre and geography.

For the report, WARM ranked the Global Top 100 dance tracks over the first six months of 2026 using airplay data from 218 dedicated dance radio stations in 39 countries. The panel of stations includes BBC Radio 1 and NTS Radio in the United Kingdom, SiriusXM’s BPM and Diplo’s Revolution and Ibiza Global Radio in Spain.

ANOTR’s “Talk to You,” featuring 54 Ultra, was the most played track of the half of 2026 with 15,087 plays. The song, which spent 17 weeks at No. 1 on the weekly WARM Global Dance Airplay chart, edges out Sonny Fodera, D.O.D and Poppy Baskcomb’s “Think About Us” (No. 2; 12,908 plays) and HUGEL and SOLTO’s “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” (No. 3; 11,791).

Artists from 26 countries across six continents are represented in the top 100, though the U.K. and U.S. are the anchors, as U.K. artists account for 25.6% of artist appearances and U.S. artists account for 20.7%. Still, the rest of the world makes up the majority, with 53.7% of appearances. France (9.4%), Germany and the Netherlands (6.9% each) head up that group, while acts from countries including South Korea, Brazil, Nigeria and Zimbabwe also earn spots.

On the genre side, dance pop leads with 40 tracks, or 38.8% of the chart. House (17 songs) and tech house (12) follow, and together the top three genres make up two-thirds of the list. In all, the top 100 spans 17 genres, with Afro house (10 titles) close behind the leaders.

“Talk to You” is the most played track in WARM’s Global Top 100 for the first half of 2026, with 15,087 plays across 218 dedicated dance radio stations worldwide. That puts it about 2,200 plays ahead of the No. 2, “Think About Us” (12,908), and nearly 3,300 ahead of No. 3 “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” (11,791).

It’s also the only title that ANOTR and 54 Ultra each has in the top 100, so it accounts for all of their plays in the report. The song alone is enough to help them place in the top 10 artists by total plays.

entertainment.title: Jonathan Groff to Return to Broadway in Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
entertainment.summary: The play marks the third Broadway project for Groff in recent years, following 'Just In Time' and 'Merrily We Roll Along.'
entertainment.body:
Jonathan Groff is returning to Broadway this season in the solo play The Amish Project.

The play, written by Jessica Dickey, is a fictional exploration of a schoolhouse shooting in an Amish community, and how the community learns to provide forgiveness and compassion. Sarna Lapine will direct the show, which is slated to begin performances Feb. 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre.

The play debuted at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off-Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since had productions at regional theaters across the U.S. and around the world. The play is typically performed as a one-woman show, with the main actor playing multiple characters. Groff will perform the play as written. Related Stories Lifestyle Tom Hanks Sets Broadway Return in 'This World of Tomorrow' Lifestyle Daniel Kaluuya to Make U.S. Stage Debut in New Branden Jacobs-Jenkins Play

This marks the third Broadway project for Groff in recent years, following his Tony-nominated run in Just In Time from March 2025 to 2026 and his Tony-winning role in Merrily We Roll Along in the 2023-2024 season . He comes to the project after making his Royal Shakespeare Company debut in As You Like It this past fall. He recently completed production on Lin-Manuel Miranda’s feature adaptation of Octet , as well as the independent film Trust the Man , which he stars in opposite Daniel Radcliffe.

The subject matter of the play struck a chord with Groff, who grew up nearby in Amish country.

“20 years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team,” Groff said.

Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, producers of Just In Time , are producing the play.

With two songs on the Billboard Hot 100 right now, Adéla is having a real moment, and she’s waving the flag for her homeland, Slovakia.

If it all feels unreal, bizarre even, Adéla can be forgiven. Ever since she learned to read and write, her mind has been occupied with the American dream. As a youngster, the Disney Channel was constantly switched on at the family home, Adéla hatched a plan and a timeline.

“I basically wanted to be famous,” she told host Jimmy Fallon, when she stopped by NBC’s The Tonight Show for the Thursday (Oct. 22) episode. Her education included watching the comedian’s interviews with Ariana Grande, Miley Cyrus and others. Explore Adéla See latest videos, charts and news

She wrote a song called ‘Nicole Kidman,’” the Oscar winner remarked at the time . “She’s so talented.” Related Tate McRae Debuts at No. 1 In Australia With 'Housewife' LISA, Miley, Kacey Musgraves & John Mayer: New Music Friday Guide Cristian Castro Accepts the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award 'In the Name of Romantic Love'

entertainment.title: Judge Orders Trump to Testify Under Oath in BBC Defamation Lawsuit
entertainment.summary: The President could face sanctions if he fails to answer questions by the December deadline.
entertainment.body:
Logo text A U.S. judge has told Donald Trump that he must answer questions in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC or face sanctions.

If the President does not sit for a deposition under oath by Dec. 11, the most extreme outcome might include the dismissal of the entire suit, according to the BBC .

Last year, Trump sued the British broadcaster over claims that a BBC Panorama documentary was doctored to make it appear as though Trump, during his Jan. 6, 2021 speech outside the White House, had urged his followers to attack the Capitol. The 33-page document, brought in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida last December, alleges that the BBC made “a false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump.”

A BBC spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter as news of the lawsuit broke: “While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree [that] there is a basis for a defamation claim.”

Ten months later, Trump cancelled a previous deposition set for Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” A lawyer for the BBC said in court that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia and had “prioritized that” over answering questions.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by Dec. 11 or he’ll face sanctions, unless this “discovery period” — described by the BBC as the phase where both sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence — is extended.

All of this came about when a leaked BBC memo from an independent advisor, a man named Michael Prescott, concluded that the doc Trump: A Second Chance? “seemed to be taking a distinctly anti-Trump stance.”

“Housewife” becomes the Canadian pop artist’s first leader and sixth top 10 appearance on the ARIA Singles Chart . Lifted from her forthcoming fourth album, “Housewife” goes one better than McRae’s “Greedy,” which peaked at No. 2 in 2023.
